Ran cross country in high school. Tips:

  1. Run with someone else if possible. If you make plans to run with someone your more likely to keep it up. Also long distance can get boring alone.

  2. Make it routine, you can run when you feel you have time or you can make time to run. I suggest running the same time every day, it keeps me on track.

  3. Music, either hum a tune or bring a mp3 player. Music keeps a beat and can help you keep up your pace. I always hum because I like to hear nature on my runs, but a lot of other runners had ipods.

  4. Hydrate adequately the entire day not just before you run. Drinking a large amount immediately before running can cause cramps and stomach pain. If you get thirsty on runs take water with you. I never took water with me because it adds weight, and I wouldn't have water in a race either, but we trained to hydrate all day before running and after. If your not running competitively carry water.

  5. Run away from your vehicle or house till you decide to quit, then jog back. If you are not running a set amount of distance, this method forces you to get an adequate cool down period for your run. Running all out and stopping cold is painful for days afterwards. A proper cool down combined with stretching minimizes muscle fatigue and pain.

About the music. Make sure if you listen to music you aren't running on the streets. Drivers never pay any attention to what is going on and the risk of getting hit is extremely high (even without music). You need to be hyper-aware of your surroundings and expect that every car is going to hit you. That way if they do start to pull out in front of you, you are already prepared for the situation and can react quickly.

• Run Slower, longer. Take your time and let your body adapt to the things you're putting through and let that endurance build over time. You can't go into it expecting to run like you've been doing it for years. it takes time.

  • Use the feeling that you already have about how much better you feel about yourself. You ran two miles and you feel damn good, how do you think you're going to feel once you're able to go out and do an easy 8 or even if you don't get that far, how is it going to feel knowing you can do that same 2 mile run you just did and come back feeling like you could do it again?

  • Never think of it as you have to run, think of it as you get to run. Don't let the idea of running be something negative and difficult. You already made the first step, so start to think of it as a reward that you get to do today. You get to get fit and enjoy the outdoors. You're less likely to continue running if you put that negative stigma on the idea of it.

  • As @Frowning_Buffalo stated, find a running buddy or buddies. I can't tell you how difficult it is to want to train or even get better when I'm doing it by myself. It also makes that long run 10x easier when you are sticking to conversational pace next to someone. The run goes by much faster that way. Also, having someone else there keeps you both accountable to make sure that you are running.

  • Hydrate, hydrate, hydrate.

  • As I mentioned in another comment, be hyper-aware. No one pays any attention to pedestrians. I can't tell you the number of times that I have nearly been hit by a car. They're in a 3,000 pound machine and they've very important things to do. Don't expect them to always look out for you and don't assume that they know you're there. You should know what is going to happen 5 seconds before it happens so that when it does, and you are in risk of getting hurt, you are already prepared and making adjustments as necessary.

The only things I'm going to add are of practical importance.

If you're on the road for part or all of your run, make sure you are running against traffic. In America this generally means the left side of the road. This is so you can see what's coming and they can see you. If you need to dive off the road, you can react to what you see better than what you can't. The caveat to this is that around blind curves you want to have the most visibility you can, so you might be better served crossing the road.

And any workout is better than no workout. Once you get into it, going for a half hour walk is going to be better than not going because you didn't feel like running.

If you can only run for a minute, then start with that and work up. That's what couch to 5k starts with.

Just went on my first run. went on a 2 mile run which mostly turned into a walk.

I would be surprised if your first run didn't turn into a walk. You took on entirely too much, too soon. Not only are you gonna end up "killing yourself" by doing that, but you're increasing your risk of injury. Your cardiopulmonary system will adapt long before your muscles, bones, and tendons adapt! The army has studies this in response to the large numbers of running injuries they saw in their new recruits the past decade. (Most were sedentary before enlisting, then started running in boot camp - stress fractures galore!).

If you're running <2 miles, I'd check out the Couch to 5k program, it's an amazing and scientifically sound training program. It has brought me from 1 minute jogs to 30 minute runs!

  • You'll get there!
  • Yes, stay hydrated, but give your stomach time to settle so you don't get cramps. You can also bring water with you! (Remember to sip, like a fine wine, instead of chugging it.)
  • Then run slower! Even a 10 minute mile is good for a beginner! You can split your workout up like Day1: Faster intervals over shorter distances. Day2: Continuous intensity intervals, ie, your 10 minute mile. Day3: Run slower, but run longer.
  • They're bastards that really condition you and get you strong. I love hills now, they really work my butt - I hate the downhills though.

The biggest bit of advice I want to stress to you - RUN AT YOUR OWN PACE.
